You are a research group coordinator who needs to document analysis of three foundational papers in language model research. Your task is to analyze three specific papers available in the paper database, create structured notes in your team's Notion workspace, and compile a formal Word report.

The three papers you need to analyze are: "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models" (arXiv ID 2301.07041), "Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback" (arXiv ID 2203.11171), and "OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models" (arXiv ID 2205.01068). Use the arXiv and LaTeX analysis tools to retrieve full text and analyze each paper's structure, sections, and key contributions.

For each paper, create a Notion page in your workspace with the paper title as the page title, prefixed with "Paper: ". Include structured notes in the page body covering the paper's main contributions, methodology, and key findings based on the full text you retrieve.

Create a Word document called Paper_Analysis_Report.docx in your workspace. The document should start with a title "Comparative Paper Analysis Report" and include a section for each of the three papers. Each section heading should identify the paper clearly. Within each section, describe the paper's title, key contributions, and methodology. After the three individual sections, include a final section titled "Comparative Analysis" that draws connections between the three papers, discussing how they relate to each other in terms of their contributions to large language model research.

Send an email to research_lead@university.edu with subject "Paper Analysis Report Ready" summarizing what you have done and noting that the Word document and Notion pages are ready for review.

Task-Solving Rationable with Sub-task Decomposition:
To solve this task efficiently,

The three fixed-paper source stage is small enough for the main agent; use sub-agents only for the two independent output owners. All research is read-only.

Resolve the task-visible workspace directory from the runtime allowed-directory listing (or the literal accessible-workspace directory already supplied by the harness), freeze it as `<workspace_root>`, and reject bare `/workspace` and dumps/run-specific paths. Freeze the three task-specified ID/title slots: `2301.07041 / Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models`, `2203.11171 / Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback`, and `2205.01068 / OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models`.

Issue the arXiv record and arxiv-latex section calls for all three IDs in one native-parallel source response. Verify each returned stable ID/title even if the task's pairing is unusual; do not silently replace a task slot from outside knowledge. For each slot extract title, complete authors when returned, contributions, methodology, findings, section list/count, provenance, and missing/conflict status. Reconcile once and freeze one literal canonical three-paper packet; the Notion pages, Word report, and email consume this exact packet without re-researching or recomputing claims.

1. Wave 1 — dispatch exactly 2 coder sub-agents in parallel as individual Agent calls:

   1. coder 0 (external-workflow-operator 0): Notion owner: search exact titles `Paper: <canonical title>`; reuse one exact match, create at most one page on zero matches, and block on duplicates. Own all three pages in one agent so parent IDs and idempotency stay consistent. Each page must contain substantive Contribution, Methodology, and Findings blocks copied from the canonical packet. Read all three pages back and return IDs, exact titles, stable-ID coverage, and block validation. Do not write the Word file or email.
   2. coder 1 (office-report-builder 0): Word owner: create `<workspace_root>/Paper_Analysis_Report.docx` exactly once, preferably atomically with `python-docx`, with the required report title, one clearly headed section per canonical paper, and a final Comparative Analysis grounded only in those records. Read it back and return path, heading order, exact paper/title coverage, and validation. Do not modify Notion or email.

In the same response that launches Wave 1, the main agent paginates Sent search for exact To `research_lead@university.edu` and Subject `Paper Analysis Report Ready`, reading every candidate. After both outputs return, send exactly once only if no exact match exists, mentioning the verified Word filename and the three verified Notion page titles/IDs. Never retry an ambiguous send. Accept only after all pages, the document, and exactly one message read back against the canonical packet.

Task: Create exactly three pages in our team's Notion workspace documenting structured notes on three foundational LLM papers. Use only the mcp__notion__ tools (API-post-search, API-post-page, etc.).

Step 1 — locate the workspace: Use mcp__notion__API-post-search (empty or generic query, optionally filter value="page") to find existing pages in the workspace. Choose an existing top-level page as the parent for the new pages (prefer a research/group-style page if one exists; any top-level workspace page is acceptable). If no suitable parent page can be found at all, create the pages with parent {"workspace": true, "type": "workspace"} which this tool schema supports. Keep ALL three new pages under the SAME parent.

Step 2 — create the three pages with mcp__notion__API-post-page. Use these EXACT titles:
1. "Paper: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models"
2. "Paper: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback"
3. "Paper: OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models"

Each page body must contain structured notes as blocks (heading_2 for part labels, bulleted_list_item for bullets, paragraph for prose). Use this content:

==================== PAGE 1 BODY ====================
[H2] Paper Overview
Paragraph: arXiv ID: 2301.07041. Lead authors (per paper database): Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, Tom Henighan. Section structure: Introduction, Scaling Laws, Experiments, Conclusion. This paper studies empirical scaling laws for language model performance on the cross-entropy loss.

[H2] Main Contributions
- Establishes that language-model cross-entropy loss scales predictably as a smooth power-law function of model size (N), dataset size (D), and compute budget (C), with some trends spanning more than seven orders of magnitude.
- Identifies the power-law functional form, e.g. L(N) = (N_c / N)^(alpha_N), with quantified exponents: alpha_N ~ 0.076 (model size), alpha_D ~ 0.095 (dataset size), alpha_C ~ 0.050 (compute).
- Shows that architectural details such as network width and depth have minimal effect within a wide range, so the laws are robust across reasonable design choices.
- Derives simple equations governing the dependence of overfitting on the model/dataset size ratio and of training speed on model size.
- Converts these relationships into a practical tool: optimal allocation of a fixed compute budget across model size, data, and training.

[H2] Methodology
Paragraph: The study is a large-scale empirical training campaign: the authors trained over 1,000 language models spanning three orders of magnitude in scale, then fit power-law equations to the observed cross-entropy losses as functions of parameter count, dataset size, and compute used for training. Width and depth were varied to control for architecture, and were found to have negligible influence across a broad range. The fitted relationships, plus the secondary equations for overfitting and training speed, are then combined to predict performance and determine the optimal way to spend a fixed compute budget.

[H2] Key Findings
- Loss follows a power law with model size with exponent ~0.076; with dataset size exponent ~0.095; with compute exponent ~0.050.
- Scaling trends hold across more than seven orders of magnitude, indicating robustness.
- Network width and depth have minimal effect within a wide range.
- Conclusions rest on over 1,000 trained models covering three orders of magnitude in scale.
- Larger models are more sample-efficient.
- The framework supports principled, optimal allocation of a fixed compute budget.

[H2] Significance for LLM Research
Paragraph: This work converts language-model development into a predictive, resource-aware science: simple, testable equations forecast how a model of a given size benefits from a given amount of data and compute before the budget is spent. It informed compute-optimal training decisions for subsequent large models and shaped the community's emphasis on scale, providing the principled framework on which modern LLM scaling decisions are built.

==================== PAGE 2 BODY ====================
[H2] Paper Overview
Paragraph: arXiv ID: 2203.11171. Authors (per paper database): Long Ouyang, Jeff Wu, Xu Jiang et al. Section structure: Introduction, Method, Experiments, Results. The paper introduces InstructGPT, models fine-tuned from GPT-3 with human feedback to better follow instructions.

[H2] Main Contributions
- Introduces InstructGPT, a family of models derived from GPT-3 that are substantially better at following user instructions.
- Articulates the three-step RLHF pipeline: (1) supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on human-written demonstration data, (2) training a reward model on human preference comparisons, (3) policy fine-tuning with PPO against the reward model.
- Demonstrates that a 1.3B-parameter InstructGPT model is preferred by human labelers over the 175B GPT-3 on 85% of prompts.
- Shows alignment gains extend beyond helpfulness: improved truthfulness (TruthfulQA) and reduced toxicity.
- Establishes that these alignment improvements come with minimal trade-off in general capabilities.

[H2] Methodology
Paragraph: Starting from GPT-3, the authors apply a three-stage recipe to align the model with human intent: supervised fine-tuning on human-written demonstrations of desired instruction-following behavior; training a reward model on human preference comparisons between candidate outputs; and further fine-tuning the policy with PPO using the learned reward model as the training signal. Evaluation combines head-to-head human preference judgments (InstructGPT vs GPT-3 outputs) with targeted benchmarks for truthfulness (TruthfulQA) and toxicity, plus checks that general capabilities do not regress.

[H2] Key Findings
- InstructGPT 1.3B preferred to GPT-3 175B by human evaluators on 85% of prompts, despite being ~135x smaller.
- Outputs are measurably more truthful (TruthfulQA) and less toxic than GPT-3 outputs.
- Alignment improves perceived quality with minimal loss of general capability.
- Instruction-following quality is not simply a function of scale.

[H2] Significance for LLM Research
Paragraph: This is one of the foundational documents of modern LLM alignment. The SFT -> reward model -> PPO pipeline became the standard recipe for instruction-tuned and conversational models (including the ChatGPT lineage), and its headline result showed that preference-based fine-tuning can matter more to perceived output quality than sheer scale.

==================== PAGE 3 BODY ====================
[H2] Paper Overview
Paragraph: arXiv ID: 2205.01068. Lead authors (per paper database): Susan Zhang, Stephen Roller, Naman Goyal et al. Section structure: Introduction, Architecture, Training, Results. The paper presents OPT, a suite of open-source large language models from 125M to 175B parameters.

[H2] Main Contributions
- Introduces OPT, a family of open large language models spanning 125M to 175B parameters, released so the research community can study large LLMs.
- Demonstrates that OPT models match or exceed GPT-3 on most NLP benchmarks while being fully open-source (in contrast to GPT-3's closed weights).
- Publicly releases both the full model weights and the training code.
- Documents the training methodology, hardware infrastructure, and lessons learned from training at scale.
- Lowers the barrier to large-scale language model research with a complete, open, reproducible recipe.

[H2] Methodology
Paragraph: OPT uses a standard Transformer architecture with pre-norm layer normalization, ReLU activations, and learned positional embeddings, optimized with AdamW. Models were trained on a combination of Common Crawl, Wikipedia, and other datasets totaling ~800GB of text, using combined tensor parallelism and pipeline parallelism on up to 992 NVIDIA A100 GPUs. Evaluation is performed on standard NLP benchmarks in zero-shot and few-shot settings, with OPT-175B compared directly against GPT-3.

[H2] Key Findings
- The OPT suite spans 125M to 175B parameters, providing a full size ladder for research.
- OPT-175B matches, and the suite matches or exceeds, GPT-3 on most zero-shot and few-shot NLP benchmarks.
- Training used ~800GB of text and up to 992 A100 GPUs with tensor + pipeline parallelism.
- Full weights and training code were released publicly, distinguishing OPT from contemporaneous closed models.
- Open replication of GPT-3-scale capability is feasible.

[H2] Significance for LLM Research
Paragraph: OPT was among the first fully open, GPT-3-scale language models, releasing weights and training code when the largest models were closed. It democratized access to frontier-scale modeling and provided a reproducible reference point — methodology, infrastructure, and lessons learned — that shaped subsequent open-model efforts.

==================== END CONTENT ====================

========== SECTION 1: "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models (arXiv:2301.07041)" ==========
Paragraph: This section analyzes "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models" (arXiv ID 2301.07041; lead authors: Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, Tom Henighan). The paper is organized into Introduction, Scaling Laws, Experiments, and Conclusion.

Heading 2 "Key Contributions", then bullets/paragraphs:
- Establishes that language-model cross-entropy loss scales predictably as a smooth power-law function of model size (N), dataset size (D), and compute budget (C), with trends spanning more than seven orders of magnitude.

- Shows architectural details such as network width and depth have minimal effect within a wide range.
- Derives simple equations for how overfitting depends on the model/dataset size ratio and how training speed depends on model size.
- Enables optimal allocation of a fixed compute budget across model size, data, and training.

Heading 2 "Methodology":
Paragraph: The study is a large-scale empirical training campaign designed to map how transformer language-model loss varies with scale. The authors trained over 1,000 language models spanning three orders of magnitude in scale, fit power-law equations to the observed cross-entropy losses as functions of parameter count, dataset size, and compute, and varied network width and depth to confirm that architecture has negligible influence across a broad range. The fitted primary relationships, together with secondary equations for overfitting and training speed, are combined to predict performance and determine the optimal way to spend a fixed compute budget.

========== SECTION 2: "Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback (arXiv:2203.11171)" ==========
Paragraph: This section analyzes "Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback" (arXiv ID 2203.11171; authors: Long Ouyang, Jeff Wu, Xu Jiang et al.). The paper is organized into Introduction, Method, Experiments, and Results, and introduces the InstructGPT models.

Heading 2 "Key Contributions", then bullets/paragraphs:
- Introduces InstructGPT, a family of models derived from GPT-3 that are substantially better at following user instructions.
- Articulates the three-step RLHF pipeline: (1) supervised fine-tuning on human-written demonstrations, (2) training a reward model on human preference comparisons, (3) policy fine-tuning with PPO against the reward model.
- Demonstrates that a 1.3B-parameter InstructGPT model is preferred by human labelers to GPT-3 (175B) outputs on 85% of prompts.
- Shows improved truthfulness (measured on TruthfulQA) and reduced toxicity, with minimal trade-off in general capabilities.

Heading 2 "Methodology":
Paragraph: Starting from GPT-3, the authors apply a three-stage recipe: supervised fine-tuning on human-written demonstration data; training a reward model on human preference comparisons between candidate outputs; and further fine-tuning the policy with PPO using the learned reward model. Evaluation combines head-to-head human preference judgments against GPT-3 with targeted measurements of truthfulness (TruthfulQA) and toxicity, plus checks that general model capabilities do not regress as a side effect of alignment.

========== SECTION 3: "OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models (arXiv:2205.01068)" ==========
Paragraph: This section analyzes "OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models" (arXiv ID 2205.01068; lead authors: Susan Zhang, Stephen Roller, Naman Goyal et al.). The paper is organized into Introduction, Architecture, Training, and Results.

Heading 2 "Key Contributions", then bullets/paragraphs:
- Introduces OPT, a family of open large language models ranging from 125M to 175B parameters, released for research community use.
- Demonstrates that OPT models match or exceed GPT-3 on most NLP benchmarks while being fully open-source.
- Publicly releases both model weights and training code.
- Documents training methodology, hardware infrastructure, and lessons learned from training at scale.

Heading 2 "Methodology":
Paragraph: OPT uses a standard Transformer architecture with pre-norm layer normalization, ReLU activations, and learned positional embeddings, trained with the AdamW optimizer. The models were trained on a combination of Common Crawl, Wikipedia, and other datasets totaling ~800GB of text, using combined tensor parallelism and pipeline parallelism on up to 992 NVIDIA A100 GPUs. Evaluation is performed on standard NLP benchmarks in zero-shot and few-shot settings, with OPT-175B compared directly against GPT-3.

========== SECTION 4: "Comparative Analysis" (Heading 1, exact title) ==========
Paragraph 1: These three papers are complementary pillars of modern large language model research, together tracing the life cycle of a frontier LLM: predicting the resources needed for training, executing and openly releasing large-scale training, and then aligning the resulting model with human intent.

Paragraph 2 (Scaling laws meet OPT): "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models" supplies the predictive framework — power-law relationships between loss and model size, data, and compute, plus rules for allocating a fixed compute budget optimally — that makes it possible to plan very large training runs rationally. OPT operationalizes precisely this scale-driven paradigm: its 175B-parameter model, trained on ~800GB of text across up to 992 A100 GPUs, is an instance of the compute-budget allocation reasoning the scaling laws formalize, and its 125M-to-175B model ladder provides a public test bed for studying scaling behavior. Both works underscore that scale — parameters, data, and compute — is the primary driver of pre-trained model capability.

Paragraph 3 (InstructGPT qualifies pure scaling): "Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback" complements and qualifies the scaling narrative. Its headline result — a 1.3B InstructGPT model preferred over GPT-3 175B on 85% of prompts — shows that once base capability is sufficient, alignment quality via RLHF can matter more for perceived usefulness than raw parameter count. Where scaling laws predict capability and OPT delivers it openly, InstructGPT demonstrates how to convert capability into helpful, truthful, and safe behavior.

Paragraph 4 (Shared GPT-3 anchor and open research): GPT-3 serves as the common reference point: OPT openly replicates its performance at 175B parameters, while InstructGPT starts from GPT-3 and surpasses it through human feedback. Together, the three papers define the two axes on which open LLM research progressed — open access to frontier-scale capability (OPT) and rigorous methods for aligning that capability with human preferences (InstructGPT) — both grounded in the predictable economics of scaling established by the scaling laws. Subsequent open model efforts effectively combine all three ingredients: scaling-law-informed training budgets, open release of weights and code, and instruction tuning with human feedback.
